query: For pregnant women with hypertension or impaired fetal growth, what are the effects of antenatal abdominal decompression on perinatal outcomes?
response: [[[Based on a Cochrane systematic review (Hofmeyr 2012) that pooled three small randomized trials from 1967–1973 (total N≈356) in pregnant women with hypertension and/or suspected fetal compromise, antenatal abdominal decompression was associated with statistically significant reductions in persistent pre-eclampsia (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.18–0.72), fetal distress in labour (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.19–0.71), low birthweight (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.40–0.63), low Apgar scores at one minute (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.12–0.56), and perinatal mortality (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.22–0.71). However, all three included trials have serious methodological shortcomings—quasi-random allocation (e.g., alternation), lack of blinding, potential selection and reporting biases, and very small sample sizes—which substantially undermine confidence in these effect estimates. The striking apparent benefits on birthweight and perinatal mortality must therefore be interpreted with considerable caution. No new trials have been reported in the subsequent five decades, and a 2019 NICE evidence review found no additional evidence on abdominal decompression for pre-eclampsia. A separate Cochrane review of prophylactic abdominal decompression in normal pregnancy showed no benefit and a possible signal of harm (non-significant increase in perinatal mortality). In summary, although the limited available data suggest a potential for improved perinatal outcomes, the evidence is too old, methodologically weak, and imprecise to support clinical use; well-designed contemporary randomized controlled trials are needed before antenatal abdominal decompression can be recommended for women with hypertension or impaired fetal growth.]]]
